note.explanation: Atoms form bonds because combining can lower their energy and make them more stable. Sodium can lose one electron more easily than it can gain seven; hydrogen can lose one electron or gain one electron to complete a duplet.
examples: Sodium loses one electron rather than gaining seven to complete its octet.
Hydrogen can gain one electron to form H⁻ and complete its duplet.
note.checkAnswer: Atoms form bonds to lower their energy and increase their stability.
note.simple: Atoms can become more stable by combining with other atoms. They tend to complete the number of electrons in their outermost shell: two for a duplet or eight for an octet.
note.checkQuestion: Why does sodium lose one electron instead of gaining seven?
note.title: Why atoms form chemical bonds
steps: Check how many electrons the atom needs to complete its outermost shell.
Consider whether losing or gaining electrons is the energetically easier path.
The atom can form a bond by taking that easier path.
note.answer: Atoms form chemical bonds to lower their energy and increase their stability.

options: To lower their energy and become more stable
mcqs.stem: According to Section 3.1, why do atoms combine with other atoms?
rationales: Combining does not make atoms seek higher energy.
Correct: combining can lower an atom’s energy and increase its stability.
Bonding does not change the size of an atom’s nucleus.
Atoms may attain a stable outer shell, but they do not become noble-gas atoms.

mcqs.stem: How many electrons are in the outermost shell of helium?
rationales: Helium’s outermost shell contains two electrons, not one.
Correct: helium has two electrons in its outermost shell.
Eight electrons are in the outermost shells of the other noble gases described in the section.
The section states that helium has two outermost-shell electrons.

options: They are stable and generally unreactive
mcqs.stem: What is given as the probable reason that noble gases do not usually combine with themselves or other atoms?
rationales: The section says noble gases do not combine with themselves.
Correct: their stability is given as the probable reason for their lack of reactivity.
Noble gases do have electrons; helium has two and the others discussed have eight in their outermost shells.
The section does not say that noble gases lose eight electrons.

mcqs.stem: What name was given to the principle that two outermost-shell electrons for hydrogen and helium, or eight for other atoms, mean stability?
rationales: Duplet describes the two-electron case but not the eight-electron case.
Octet describes the eight-electron case but not the two-electron case.
Correct: the section names the principle the Duplet or Octet Rule.
This is not the name given to the principle in the section.

mcqs.stem: Which path does a sodium atom take to reach a stable arrangement, according to the section?
rationales: Correct: the section says it is easier for sodium to lose one electron.
The section contrasts losing one electron with gaining seven and says losing one is easier.
The section does not say sodium gains eight electrons.
The section says sodium loses one electron, not seven.

mcqs.stem: Which hydrogen ion completes a duplet by gaining one electron?
rationales: H⁺ forms when hydrogen loses one electron.
Correct: H⁻ forms when hydrogen gains one electron and completes its duplet.
The section describes hydrogen forming H⁺ or H⁻, not H₂⁺ in this example.
The section does not identify H₂⁻ as the result of hydrogen gaining one electron.

written.text: What type of elements lose their outer electron easily and what type of elements gain electron easily?
written.finalAnswer: Electropositive metals lose outer electrons easily; electronegative non-metals gain electrons easily.

rubric.how: Name metals and state that they lose outer electrons.

rubric.why: Identifying the elements that gain electrons earns the second mark.
rubric.description: State that electronegative non-metals gain electrons easily.

modelAnswer: Electropositive metals lose outer electrons easily.

written.text: Explain the formation of an ionic bond and a covalent bond.
written.finalAnswer: An ionic bond forms by electron transfer and electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; a covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons.

rubric.why: An ionic bond begins with electron transfer.
rubric.description: Explain that electrons are transferred between atoms to form ions.
rubric.how: State that one atom loses electron(s) and another gains them.

rubric.why: The opposite charges explain the attraction in an ionic bond.
rubric.description: Identify the oppositely charged ions formed.

rubric.why: Sharing electrons is the key formation step for a covalent bond.
rubric.description: Explain that atoms share electrons to form a covalent bond.
rubric.how: Use the idea of a shared pair or shared electrons.

rubric.why: The answer must connect electron sharing to the covalent bond being asked about.
rubric.description: State that the shared electrons hold the atoms together in a covalent bond.
rubric.how: Link the shared electrons to the formation of the bond.

modelAnswer: An ionic bond forms when electrons are transferred from one atom to another, forming positive and negative ions.
The oppositely charged ions attract each other.
A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons.
The shared electrons hold the atoms together in a covalent bond.

examTips: A short-answer question may ask which types of elements lose or gain electrons; name both the element type and what it does.
A descriptive question may ask why atoms form bonds. Link bond formation to lowering energy and increasing stability.
For an answer about the duplet or octet rule, give the electron count correctly: two for the first shell and eight for the outermost shells of the other noble gases discussed.
In a longer answer, distinguish electron loss or gain from electron sharing; do not describe both as the same process.

hints: Metals are electropositive and tend to lose electrons; non-metals are electronegative and tend to gain them.

steps.why: The section explains that sodium can become stable by taking the easier of two possible electron changes.
steps.text: For sodium atom it is easy to lose one electron and stabilize itself than to gain seven electrons while completing its octet.

steps.why: This states the energetically easier route sodium takes to form a bond.
steps.text: Sodium atom, therefore, adopts the energetically easier path and loses its electron to form a bond.

example.question: Why does sodium lose one electron rather than gain seven electrons to complete its octet?
example.answer: Sodium loses one electron because this is energetically easier than gaining seven electrons, and it stabilizes the atom.

explain.title: Atoms form bonds to become more stable
explain.body: Atoms have a tendency to decrease their energy. They can do this by combining with other atoms. It is a natural phenomenon because it increases the stability of atoms.

explain.title: Duplet and octet
explain.body: The section states: “This principle was named as Duplet or Octet Rule.” Two electrons in the outermost shell give the duplet for hydrogen and helium; eight electrons give the octet for the other noble gases discussed.

explain.title: Atoms take an easier electron path
explain.body: Atoms can lose or gain electrons to complete an outer shell. Sodium loses one electron rather than gaining seven because losing one is energetically easier.

explain.title: Hydrogen can form either ion
explain.body: The section explains that hydrogen can lose one electron to become H⁺ or gain one electron to become H⁻; in the latter case, it completes its duplet.

mistakes: Saying that helium has eight electrons in its outermost shell; it has two.
Confusing the duplet with the octet: a duplet has two electrons and an octet has eight.
Writing that sodium gains seven electrons; the section says sodium loses one because that is easier.
Saying that atoms form bonds to increase their energy; the section says they tend to decrease their energy.
Naming only metals or non-metals without stating whether they lose or gain electrons.
